Experience curves (or learning curves) describe how the unit cost of a technology falls as its cumulative installed capacity or production grows, usually expressed as a learning rate, the fractional cost reduction per doubling of cumulative capacity. Installed capacity acts as a proxy for R&D, learning by doing and learning by using, so these curves are used for "top down" forecasts of future costs that complement "bottom up" engineering-economic estimates. New technologies often show a cost rise during early commercialization before the decline sets in. See also [CO2 Capture](/papers/topics/co2-capture/).

## Experience curves for CO2 capture cost forecasting (2012)

Rubin et al. used the historical record of power plant SO2 and NOx controls as a benchmark for carbon capture ([Rubin et al. 2012](/papers/rubin2012/)). Capital costs of wet FGD and SCR systems rose during early commercialization and then fell by about 13% per doubling of installed capacity, and by 50% or more after about two decades of deployment; FGD SO2 removal efficiency rose from about 70% to 95% between 1969 and 1995. Applying such learning rates to the components of PC, NGCC, IGCC and oxyfuel plants with capture suggests electricity cost reductions of up to about 30% after 100 GW of capture capacity worldwide, comparable to the high end of DOE engineering estimates. The authors stress that these reductions depend on deployment, which in turn requires a policy-created market. Summary: [rubin2012](/papers/rubin2012/).
